[20:51] First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40 on page 8.

[21:56] Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

[22:03] So now we're going to look at some of the reasons why it's beneficial to include

[22:09] drama activities such as role play in your teaching practice in a range of subject areas.

[22:16] There's a lot of evidence to show that drama helps a child's personal development.

[22:20] First, creating the space for children to express themselves freely in a group situation

[22:27] helps to give them confidence in their own opinions and ideas, and of course, drama activities

[22:34] can work especially well for shy or introverted children who usually don't participate in

[22:41] other types of classroom situations.

[22:45] Secondly, unscripted improvisation activities where children work from their

[22:51] imagination, if done in a supportive way, give children the opportunity to gain

[22:57] experience in taking risks and encourage them to say things that they might

[23:02] normally be afraid to say. Drama can also support the child's educational

[23:09] development. For example, the emphasis placed on cooperative activities in

[23:15] drama means that group members must learn the value of listening to one another.

[23:21] Being involved in any sort of performance which relies on everyone working together and

[23:27] playing their part also helps children to be responsible, not only for their learning,

[23:32] but for their general behavior.

[23:35] These are just a couple of ways in which drama can benefit a child's learning.

[23:45] Now I'd like to look at how role play can be such a valuable learning tool in the classroom.

[23:52] The value of role play for children who are having difficulties as a means of therapy

[23:57] is now widely accepted.

[24:00] The experience of doing a role play where children act out aspects of their own life without

[24:06] explicitly stating that it is a direct representation of their own experiences can help children

[24:12] to judge their own behavior in an objective way.

[24:17] One obvious example would be doing a role reversal with a bully role-playing a victim.

[24:23] Because this approach doesn't involve direct confrontation, it may help the bully to see

[24:28] his or her behavior in a different light.

[24:32] More generally, role-play also allows the teacher to explore potentially controversial

[24:38] or taboo subjects in a safe setting in which children feel at ease.

[24:44] It's obviously essential for children to feel they won't be criticized or judged for voicing certain views.

[24:53] Getting children to examine their thoughts and opinions carefully can lead to a deeper self-knowledge and a stronger awareness of morality.

[25:02] This is an important factor in developing social skills.

[25:07] Let's look at a specific subject area now and think about how drama can enrich the learning

[25:13] process for the study of history.

[25:16] Bringing characters from the past to life in the classroom by doing classroom drama

[25:21] activities is an easy way to improve the level of the children's participation in

[25:27] the lesson.

[25:28] So drama in the history classroom makes for a livelier atmosphere, but getting children

[25:35] Children to reenact scenes from history can also be extremely useful, as it helps them

[25:40] to remember what happened and why it was important, as well as helping to bring the past alive.

[25:48] Another way of doing this is to ask children to find solutions to historical problems using

[25:55] role-play.

[25:57] This can help to focus attention on why certain decisions were taken.

[26:01] For example, children can be asked to decide how best to defend their town from attack,

[26:08] or where to build a new settlement.

[26:11] Okay, what I'd like to do now is to think about your next teaching practice session

[26:16] and in groups discuss how you would incorporate an element of drama into your lesson plan.
